The Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC), the country’s communications regulator, accused the technology giant of failing to take adequate action against harmful online materials despite repeated reports and regulatory interventions.
The regulator said the lawsuits were intended to address what it described as Google’s systemic failure to tackle harmful content and recover the substantial financial and human resources deployed to address more than 50,000 problematic online materials.
According to the commission, the first lawsuit centres on Google’s alleged failure to take appropriate measures against thousands of harmful online materials, including content promoting online gambling, scams and fraud.
The second case concerns Google’s alleged failure to take statutory and proactive measures to prevent the republication of prohibited content on YouTube by Malaysian blogger Wan Muhammad Azri Wan Deris, popularly known as Papagomo.
The content was reportedly subject to an interim injunction issued by the Kuala Lumpur High Court, but the regulator alleged that similar materials continued to circulate on the platform.
MCMC is seeking 300 million ringgit in each lawsuit, comprising 100 million ringgit in general damages, 100 million ringgit in aggravated damages and another 100 million ringgit in exemplary damages. While providing details of the regulatory concerns, it disclosed that it submitted 74,703 reports to YouTube over harmful content between January and October 2026, with 74,569, representing 99.8 per cent, relating to online gambling.
The commission said, of the gambling-related reports, YouTube responded or removed the reported content within 24 hours in 32,781 cases, while 4,950 reports received no response.
It further disclosed that 1,468 cases took more than 30 days to receive a response or have the content removed, while 35 cases exceeded 90 days.
The regulator argued that the figures demonstrated the scale of harmful content on the platform and delays in addressing materials reported for violating applicable laws and platform regulations.
“The damages sought are intended to remedy the substantial resources and manpower expended in addressing more than 50,000 harmful online content arising from Google’s systemic failure and to ensure a safe social media platform,” the commission said.
It maintained that social media platforms operating in Malaysia were subject to the country’s Communications and Multimedia Act 1998 and Online Safety Act 2025, alongside applicable licensing requirements.
The commission also urged digital platforms to strengthen their content moderation systems and comply with statutory obligations, warning that it would continue to pursue legal action against companies that failed to address harmful materials.
However, YouTube has defended its approach to content moderation, saying it remains committed to providing a safe online environment while protecting freedom of expression and access to information.
A YouTube spokesperson said the company complied with applicable laws in countries where it operates and reviewed content reported as violating its policies.
“We comply with applicable local laws in every country where we operate and thoroughly review all content flagged against our policies. We are engaging with the government on these matters,” the spokesperson said.
The lawsuits come amid growing regulatory scrutiny of major technology companies across Southeast Asia, particularly over their responsibility for content distributed through social media and video-sharing platforms.
Malaysia has previously raised concerns over the handling of harmful content by other digital platforms, including TikTok and Meta-owned Facebook, as authorities seek stronger accountability from technology companies operating within the country.
The legal action also comes against the backdrop of Google’s expanding investment interests in Malaysia. The company recently announced plans to invest $15 billion in the country between 2027 and 2028, covering data centre campuses, clean energy, water security and workforce development.
The dispute is expected to further intensify discussions around the responsibilities of global technology companies, the effectiveness of content moderation systems and the extent to which national regulators can enforce local laws on international digital platforms.
For the global technology industry, the case highlights the growing regulatory expectation that platforms must do more than provide spaces for users to publish and share content, but also establish effective mechanisms for identifying, reviewing and removing materials that violate national laws.
As governments intensify efforts to tackle online fraud, gambling promotions and other harmful digital activities, the outcome of the Malaysian lawsuits could add to the debate over platform accountability, user protection and the balance between online safety and freedom of expression.
